newsitem.title: USA: Bill asks sharply higher US beer, wine taxes.
newsitem.headline: Bill asks sharply higher US beer, wine taxes.

text.p: The federal tax on beer would double and it would triple on wine under a bill proposed Tuesday by Delegate Eleanar Holmes Norton to tax beer and wine at the same rate as hard liquor.
Norton described the bill as an attempt to curtail teenage drinking and an antidote to a beer industry proposal to roll back a 1991 tax increase.

"Teens are price sensitive because they have less disposable income," said Norton, Democrat who represents the District of Columbia in the U.S. House. "By taxing beer and wine substantially less than liquor, we bring the price down and encourage teens to make these the drinks of choice."

An additional $4 billion in taxes would be collected annually if the bill was enacted, said Michael Jacobson, head of the consumer group Center for Science in the Public Interest. CSPI said it supported the bill.

Tax on a 12-ounce can of beer, now roughly five cents, would double, Jacobson said, and the four-cent tax on a glass of table wine would triple. By comparison, tax on a 1.4-ounce glass of 80 proof liquor is 12 cents.
Norton's bill called for annual adjustment of beer and wine taxes to reflect inflation. She said she hoped to arrange a companion bill in the Senate.
The National Council on Alcoholism and Drug Dependence said studies indicated small increases in beer prices would reduce drinking by 11 percent in the 16-21-year-old group.
Mothers Against Drunk Driving and the Latino Council on Alcohol and Tobacco also supported the bill.
